disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food in a discrete period, accompanied by a subjective sense of loss of control over eating. Episodes are typically followed by marked distress, guilt, or shame, but—unlike bulimia nervosa—there are no regular inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as purging, excessive exercise, or fasting. The disorder often emerges in adolescence or early adulthood but can appear later in life, and its course can be chronic or fluctuate with stress, mood, and life transitions. It is commonly associated with obesity and metabolic problems but can occur at any weight, and it must be distinguished from occasional overeating or culturally normative feasting by its frequency, loss of control, and associated psychological distress.

narrative.stressor: Alejandro’s binge eating became clinically significant over the four months after he underwent a minor cardiac workup for chest discomfort and was told to restrict certain foods and limit portions due to rising blood pressure and weight. Already retired and spending long stretches alone at home while his wife picked up extra caregiving duties for an ailing sister, he poured himself into drafting his bilingual home‑maintenance handbook and increasingly relied on elaborate cooking sessions as his main break from the work. The more his cardiologist emphasized dietary control, the more he found himself retreating to the kitchen late in the evening, preparing oversized batches of his favorite spicy dishes and eating far beyond what he had planned, especially when he was alone and restless after a day of quiet writing and birdwatching. He finally agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of his primary‑care doctor when repeated lab visits showed further weight gain despite his insistence that he was “mostly eating healthy,” and he admitted that his eating felt out of control during solitary nights after medical appointments.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I lose control around food at night and just keep eating even when I tell myself to stop.

narrative.stressor: For Jaime, the binge eating escalated during a four‑month stretch when her junior financial manager role suddenly expanded and coincided with a demanding semester of college courses. She was working late on budgeting cycles, commuting to campus for exams, and still trying to maintain her volunteer commitments and social life, leaving her with little structured time for regular meals and almost no downtime outside of spreadsheets and deadlines. As pressure mounted—especially after a critical presentation to senior staff and a near‑miss on an important exam—she began spending long, unscheduled evenings alone in her small apartment, ordering large quantities of takeout while watching shows or half‑heartedly studying, then feeling overwhelmed by how disconnected her eating felt from actual hunger. The pattern became so disruptive that she started skipping social outings and salsa nights out of embarrassment about how she ate afterward, and she ultimately sought psychiatric help after her supervisor gently commented on her exhausted appearance and she broke down describing how her late‑night eating felt increasingly out of control.
narrative.chief_complaint: When I’m stressed after work and classes, I end up eating way more food in one sitting than seems normal for anyone.

narrative.stressor: Demetrius noticed his eating change over a four‑month period after his wife took on extra shifts and evening classes, leaving him home alone most nights after his own late retail shifts. Their usual shared dinners and weekend cooking projects gave way to him grabbing quick food on the way home, then lingering in the kitchen while listening to vinyl and sketching, repeatedly going back for more food even though he wasn’t particularly hungry. The combination of irregular hours, the temporary sense of disconnection from his wife, and his tendency to unwind solo with music made it easy for the pattern to build quietly into a routine that left him feeling physically uncomfortable and vaguely ashamed afterward. He decided to seek psychiatric care after his wife commented with concern that he seemed to be eating himself "past full" on the nights she was out, and he realized he was consistently eating until he felt stuffed and sluggish instead of relaxed after work.
narrative.chief_complaint: Most nights I end up eating until I feel uncomfortably full, even though I keep telling myself to stop earlier.
